title: Characterising extremal decoherence by quantum measurement incompatibility
authors: Daniel McNulty, William Townsend, Jukka Kiukas
abstract: Decoherence, when viewed in the Heisenberg picture, can turn incompatible measurements into jointly measurable ones. This provides an observable-level description of emergent classicality in terms of the incompatibility destroyed by a noise channel. The corresponding loss of incompatibility can be captured by the channel's \emph{compatibility region}---the observables in a probe class that become jointly measurable with every noisy observable. The geometry and volume of this region provide a refined operational way to compare noise channels. We apply this framework to decoherence channels, each of which acts by Schur multiplication with extreme points of the convex set of unit-diagonal positive semidefinite matrices. Restricting to extremals eliminates convex mixing and reveals subtle phase-dependent decoherence effects thar are not captured by damping rates or conventional coherence quantifiers. Such channels have a rigid dilation structure described by a rank-one operator frame, which reduces joint measurability to a positivity test, making the compatibility region analytically tractable, and its volume computable from the frame's Gram matrix. If the frame can be normalised to a minimal informationally complete (MIC) POVM, the compatibility region acquires a geometric interpretation in the associated probability representation of the quantum state space, familiar with Qbism. Among maximal-rank extremals, those associated with symmetric informationally complete (SIC) POVMs maximise the compatibility volume and hence destroy the greatest amount of incompatibility, providing an operational characterisation of the special role of SICs in terms of joint measurability. This leads to a new formulation of the well-known SIC existence problem as a joint measurability question for noisy mutually unbiased bases.
summary: This theoretical paper develops an observable-level measure of emergent classicality by quantifying the loss of measurement incompatibility due to decoherence. It introduces the 'compatibility region' as a key diagnostic tool, showing that high-symmetry measurements like SICs maximize this loss. The work provides rigorous mathematical frameworks for analyzing these quantum noise processes.
main_problem: The paper characterizes emergent classicality by analyzing how decoherence channels destroy quantum measurement incompatibility, providing an observable-level diagnostic tool.
main_result: Symmetric Informationally Complete (SIC) POVMs are shown to maximize the compatibility volume among extremal decoherence channels, offering a joint measurability criterion for the existence of SICs.
method: The core method involves defining and calculating the 'compatibility region' associated with noise channels acting on observables in the Heisenberg picture. This is analyzed using positivity tests derived from operator frames and Gram matrices.
model_or_system: The system models quantum decoherence via noise channels ($\Lambda_\xi$) acting on observables, particularly focusing on extremal channels defined by coherence matrices $\xi$. The analysis uses mathematical tools like rank-one operator frames and geometric interpretations in state space (related to MICs).
key_observables: Compatibility region volume, measurement incompatibility, coherence matrix ($\xi$), and the structure of POVMs (especially SICs).
important_parameters: The dimension $d$ of the Hilbert space; parameters defining the specific type of extremal channel (e.g., Heisenberg-Weyl vs. semi-SIC).
main_assumptions: The analysis heavily restricts itself to 'extremal' decoherence channels, which simplifies the structure by eliminating convex mixing effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the correspondence between symmetric extremal decoherence and SIC-POVMs, showing how joint measurability conditions translate into geometric constraints on the compatibility region in state space or Fourier space.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the incompatibility loss via the compatibility region to establishing equivalent mathematical criteria for this region's existence (especially for SIC cases). It then generalizes these findings by analyzing different classes of extremals (Heisenberg-Weyl, semi-SIC) using advanced tools like Fourier analysis and robustness measures.
why_interesting: This work provides a deep operational link between fundamental quantum concepts—measurement incompatibility and classicality—and concrete mathematical structures (like SICs), which is highly relevant for understanding open quantum systems dynamics beyond simple damping models.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Correspondence between symmetric extremal decoherence and SIC-POVMs. A SIC-POVM M determines the coherence matrix ξ, while an incoherent observable P is specified by the conditional probabilities p(j|n). The pair (P, ξ ◦QMUB) is jointly measurable iff these probabilities arise from a valid POVM F in the SIC representation, i.e. when the associated SIC Born rule expression is non-negative for every state.

FIG. 2. Characterising noise through the compatibility region CΛ[O] of a fixed “probe” class of observables O. This region consists of the probes that become jointly measurable with every noisy observable under the channel Λ. With no noise, CId[O] = Otriv; for a general noise channel, CΛ[O] lies between Otriv and O; and for incompatibility-breaking noise Γ, CΓ[O] = O. In this work, we focus on decoherence channels Λξ, for which the natural probe class is the set of incoherent observables, while the incompatibility-breaking reference channel Γ is complete dephasing.

FIG. 4. Compatibility regions Cξ[I sc 4 ], restricted to shift-covariant observables, for three semi-SIC extremals, shown in the Fourier coordinates (ˆr01, ˆr10, ˆr11) of the covariant seed distribution of Pr. The semi-SIC family is parametrised by β ∈(1/16, 1/12], with coherence matrices given in Eq. (50) and SIC endpoint at β = 1/12. For β < 1/12, the reduced symmetry splits the four outcomes into two inequivalent classes, so the compatibility region is the intersection of two ellipsoids E ± ξ defined in Eq. (F10). The blue and red transparent surfaces are E + ξ and E − ξ , and the dark region is E + ξ ∩E − ξ = Cξ[I sc 4 ]. The tetrahedron is the set of all valid incoherent observables.
